hints: Think about the very start of the reaction, when almost no product has formed yet so almost no catalyst is present.
As a little product forms, the amount of catalyst grows, so see how that must affect the rate in the middle of the reaction.
Towards the end, reactants are running out, so decide what must happen to the rate even though lots of catalyst is now present.
walkthrough:
**Think about time zero**

At the start, reactant concentration is high but product concentration is zero. That means there is no catalyst yet, so the rate starts very low, essentially at zero.

**Explain the speed-up phase**

As the reaction proceeds slowly, product is made. That product acts as a catalyst and lowers the activation energy, so the reaction gets faster and faster. This gives a rising rate curve.

Think of it as: more product = more catalyst = faster rate

**Explain the slow-down phase**

Later, even though there is plenty of catalyst, there is very little reactant left to react. Reactant concentration becomes the limiting factor, so the rate must fall back down towards zero.

Rise then fall gives a peaked curve starting at the origin.

options.A: Incorrect. This shows a high rate from the start that levels off. In autocatalysis the initial rate must be near zero because no catalytic product exists yet.
options.B: Incorrect. This shows the rate increasing then staying high and constant. This forgets that reactants are used up, so the rate cannot stay high forever, it must eventually decrease to zero.
options.C: Correct. Rate starts at zero (no catalyst), increases as catalytic product builds up, reaches a maximum, then decreases as reactants are depleted. This rise-and-fall peaked shape is characteristic of autocatalysis.
options.D: Incorrect. This shows maximum rate at time zero followed by continuous decrease. That is the curve for a normal reaction with no catalysis, where rate is highest when reactant concentration is highest.
